title: Regulation of skeletal muscle development and metabolism in broiler chickens by Urolithin A through threonine kinase 1 pathway activation

sections.abstract: Broiler skeletal muscle dysplasia is characterized by impaired muscle fiber hypertrophy and satellite cell dysfunction, leading to reduced meat yield and increased feed conversion rates, resulting in significant economic losses. With the impending global ban on β-adrenergic agonists, developing effective natural alternative treatments is an urgent requirement. Urolithin A (UA), a tannic acid metabolite derived from the gut microbiota, promotes muscle synthetic metabolism in mammals; however, its underlying mechanism in poultry remains unclear. We integrated network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and primary chicken skeletal muscle satellite cell (SMSC) culture experiments. A network pharmacology analysis identified threonine kinase1 (Akt1) as a key core target regulated by UA in muscle dysplasia. Further, KEGG enrichment analysis revealed differential clustering in the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K)–Akt1, forkhead box protein O1, and mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 signaling pathways. Molecular docking revealed that UA stably binds to the Akt1 protein (Binding energy: -7.7 kcal/mol), stabilized by hydrophobic interactions with Val164 and Met281. The key binding site for UA exhibits high conservation (96% homology) between mammalian and avian species. The 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation confirmed the stability of the complex. These findings indicate that the Akt1 pathway is closely associated with the protective role of uric acid in broiler muscle dysplasia. Primary skeletal muscle satellite cell experiments demonstrated that during SMSC proliferation, 50 μM UA upregulates mRNA levels of Akt1, mTORC1 , and forkhead box O1 , while enhancing the expression of myogenic differentiation 1 and myogenin during both proliferation and differentiation ( P < 0.05). In addition, Akt1 and phosphorylated Akt1 protein levels upregulated ( P < 0.05), confirming pathway activation. 50 μM UA regulates glucose metabolism by upregulating ( P < 0.05) and downregulating ( P < 0.05) pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 4 (proliferation/differentiation) mRNA levels and fructose-6-phosphate kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase 3 (differentiation) mRNA levels, respectively, thereby optimizing glycolysis-oxidation balance. Our research shows that UA influences skeletal muscle satellite cells proliferation and differentiation through the Akt1 pathway and alters glucose metabolism at different stages. As a natural, residue-free compound, it holds promise for enhancing skeletal muscle growth in broilers, supporting the shift towards antibiotic-free poultry. Further animal studies are needed to confirm these in vitro results.
sections.introduction:
Skeletal dysplasia in commercial broilers, which is pathologically characterized by impaired myofiber hypertrophy and dysfunction of satellite cells, results in significant economic loss due to carcass downgrades and increased feed conversion ratios ( Velleman, 2023 ). Although β-adrenergic agonists, such as ractopamine, are used to enhance chicken meat yield ( Li et al., 2020 ), they are prohibited in the European Union ( Nicoli et al., 2013 ) and China ( MARA PRC, 2011 ) due to concerns regarding residual drug detection in retail livestock products, necessitating urgent development of natural alternatives achieving similar anabolic effects without surpassing the residue threshold.

Natural polyphenol derivatives have emerged as promising candidates for sustainable livestock production. Urolithin A (UA), a gut microbiota-derived metabolite of pomegranate ellagitannins, exhibits multi-target regulatory effects on muscle homeostasis ( Zhang et al., 2023 , 2025 ), including activation of the Akt1/mTORC1/FoxO1 axis ( Fang et al., 2019 ; Fu et al., 2019 ). This aligns closely with the fact that post-hatch muscle growth in broiler chickens primarily relies on satellite cell-mediated myofibrillar hypertrophy ( Velleman, 2023 ). However, current evidence is primarily derived from mammalian models ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Su et al., 2024 ), leaving critical gaps in our understanding of its pharmacodynamics in avian species.

Post-hatch muscle development in poultry relies on hypertrophy mediated by satellite cells ( Schiaffino and Reggiani, 2011 ; Rodriguez et al., 2017 ). In chickens, skeletal muscle satellite cells (SMSCs) are located within an anatomical niche between the basal lamina and sarcolemma, where they remain quiescent until activated by nutrient signals or mechanical stimuli ( Daughtry et al., 2017 ; Tonniges et al., 2019 ; Bachman et al., 2024 ). This developmental limitation, unique to the species, underscores the importance of conducting targeted research utilizing chicken SMSC models to initially evaluate the efficacy of potential additives.

Accordingly, we utilized a comprehensive methodology integrating network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamic simulations, and in vitro functional assays using SMSCs. We aimed to investigate the potential targets and underlying molecular mechanisms, through which UA ameliorates muscular dysplasia in broilers.
sections.methods:
All animal procedures were conducted in strict compliance with the Guidelines for the Ethical Review of Laboratory Animal Welfare and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Sichuan Agricultural University, China (approval number: 20250116).

Collection of UA Targets: The isomeric simplified molecular input line entry system (SMILES) value of UA was obtained from the PubChem database, and its three-dimensional (3D) structure in the SDF format was downloaded. The isomeric SMILES value was input into the SwissTargetPrediction ( http://www.swisstargetprediction.‍ch ) and SuperPred ( https://prediction.charite.de/subpages/target_prediction.php ) databases for predicting potential targets. Additionally, the compound name was searched in the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD; http://ctdbase.org ) for identifying the associated targets. All predicted targets were standardized to the official gene names using UniProt. Duplicates were removed to compile the final list of UA targets (Supplementary Material 1).

Identification of muscle hypoplasia (MH)-related targets: The keyword "Muscle Hypoplasia" was used to search the GeneCards ( http://www.genecards.org ) and Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM; ( https://omim.org/ ) databases. The results from both databases were exported to Excel, merged, and deduplicated to generating a comprehensive list of muscle hypoplasia-associated targets (Supplementary Material 2).

Intersection targets and Venn diagram: The targets of UA were processed by taking the intersection of the UA targets and those related to Muscle Hypoplasia using the Venny v.2.1.0 mapping site; the intersecting targets were obtained (Supplementary Material 3); and the Weyen diagrams of intersecting targets of UA and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease were plotted.

Construction of protein–protein interaction (PPI) network and screening of the core targets: The intersecting targets were imported into the STRING database; “Multiple proteins” were selected; “Homo sapiens” was chosen as the species; and the PPI network diagram was constructed. Thereafter, “enable 3D bubble design” was selected to display nodes in 3D style, and “hide disconnected nodes in the network” was selected to hide nodes not connected to those of the others. The TSV format file was imported into Cytoscape v.3.10.2 for further processing the PPI network diagram; the Degree value of the nodes was assessed using the CytoNCA plugin; the node degree values (reflected by size) were analyzed in the PPI network, with color gradient and transparency parameterized by degree. Core targets were screened through centrality metrics (Degree, Betweenness, Closeness) using Centiscape v.2.2 and were subsequently mapped into the graph of the PPI network. Using the CytoNCA plugin, core targets were filtered using thresholds for Degree = 15.418, Betweenness = 90.418, and Closeness = 0.00588 (Supplementary Material 4).

Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses: Using DAVID for enrichment analysis of the intersecting targets, the result files of GO function and KEGG pathway enrichment were obtained (Supplementary Material 5) and categorized, and relatively highly significant enrichment results of GO and KEGG were screened with P <0.05 criterion. The selected results were imported into Microbiotics online website, plotted, and analyzed. A total of 575 enriched terms were identified, including 275, 68, 119, and 113 biological processes (BP), cellular components (CC), molecular functions (MF), and KEGG pathways, respectively.

Construction of the UA–target–pathway–MH network: After obtaining the potential targets of action of UA in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, the correspondence between UA, intersecting targets, pathways, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease was listed to produce network and type data (Supplementary Material 6). The data were imported into Cytoscape v.3.10.2 for constructing the graph of UA–intersecting targets–pathways–nonalcoholic steatohepatopathy network relationship, and the degree value of each node was analyzed using the CytoNCA plug-in.

The 3D structures of Akt1 ( P31750 ) and UA were obtained from the UniProt database using AlphaFold and the PubChem Compound database (5488186), respectively. An appropriate protein structure in the Protein Data Bank with the closest homology to Akt1 was searched using BLAST. The amino acid sequences were aligned using ESPript v.3.0. AutoDock Vina v.1.2.3 and AutoDockTools were used to prepare, run, and analyze the docking results. Kollman charges, solvation parameters, and polar hydrogen atoms were added to the protein structure, and Gasteiger charges were assigned to the ligands. The grid box size was set in the catalytic region of heme moiety, with a grid spacing of 0.375. Lamarckian genetic algorithm was used to search for the best conformers, with 100 docking runs for each ligand.

The Akt1–UA complex was modeled using GROMACS v.2024.2 with the AMBER14SB force field and TIP3P explicit water model. Ligand parameters were generated using sobtop. The system was solvated in a cubic box (1.2-nM buffer) and neutralized with counterions. Energy minimization (5,000 steps) employed steepest descent for eliminating atomic clashes. Equilibration involved NVT ensemble heating from 0 to 300 K over 100 ps (V-rescale thermostat) and NPT ensemble pressurization to 1 bar for 100 ps (Berendsen barostat). The bonds were constrained using LINCS, and production simulations (100 ns) utilized the leapfrog algorithm (2-fs timestep) with the particle-mesh Ewald electrostatics ( Hess et al., 2008 ).

The pectoralis major muscles were dissected from 5-day-old Ross 308 broiler chicks for SMSC isolation, following an established enzymatic dissociation protocol ( Hu et al., 2021 ). Subsequently, the cell supernatant was filtered through a cell strainer with pore sizes of 0.075 and 0.02 mm, and cells were isolated by centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 2 min. Isolated and purified cells were plated in 25 cm 3 cell culture bottles and cultured at 37°C with 5% CO 2 and saturated humidity in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). Then SMSCs were seeded in 6-well plates and cultured in GM, with six independent replicates in each treatment group in DMEM or DMEM + 50 μM UA for 24 h. When cells proliferated to 80–90%, the medium was replaced with a differentiation medium [DMEM + 2% horse serum (Gibco, NY, USA)], or differentiation medium + 50 μM UA for 72 h for inducing SMSC differentiation. The medium was replaced every 24 h, and cells were collected after 72 h. Cell viability was assessed via CCK-8 assay (Melon Bio, Dalian) to determine the optimal concentration of UA. For 24 hours, the skeletal muscle satellite cell were subjected to a variety of UA concentrations (0, 5, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, and 800 μmol/L). Each well was then filled with 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent, and the mixture was incubated for 2 h. A Varioskan LUX microplate reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) was used to measure absorbance at 450 nm. Based on our viability results and previous studies ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Wilhelmsen et al., 2025 ) , a UA concentration of 50 μM was chosen for further research.

Total RNA was isolated from cultured cells using TRIzol Reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). RNA purity and concentration were assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Wilmington, DE, USA). Genomic DNA elimination and cDNA synthesis were subsequently performed using a PrimeScript RT Reagent Kit with gDNA Eraser (TaKaRa Bio, Tokyo, Japan), according to the manufacturer's instructions.

The primers for qPCR ( Table 1 ) were designed using NCBI PrimerBlast with stringent parameters for ensuring specificity (amplicon size, 80–200 bp; Tm, 58–62°C; GC content, 40–60%). The genes expression in the primary myosatellite cells was quantified using quantitative real-time PCR. Briefly, 1 mL of the TRIzol reagent (MD020; Magen, China) was added. RNA was extracted using precooled chloroform. The supernatant was transferred to a new centrifuge tube, and isopropanol was added to precipitate the RNA. The RNA precipitate was washed twice with 75% ethanol and diluted with diethyl pyrocarbonate-treated water. All operations were performed on ice. RNA quality was determined through agarose gel electrophoresis, and the RNA was quantified using a bio-photometer (NanoDrop2000; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). In addition, 1000 ng of RNA, 5 mmol/L MgCl 2 , 1 μL of RT buffer, 1 mmol/L dNTP, 2.5 U of AMV, 0.7 nmol/L oligodeoxynucleotides d(T), and 10 U of ribonuclease inhibitor (TaKaRa, Dalian, China) were used in the reverse transcription reactions (10 μL). Real-time PCR was performed using a Bio - Rad CFXConnect ™ system ( Bio - Rad , USA). Each real-time PCR product was used as a template in a 20 μL PCR containing 0.2 μmol/L of each primer and SYBR Green premix (Accurate Biology, China); primer sequences are listed in Table S1. The PCR cycle began with a 3-min denaturation at 95°C, followed by 40 cycles: 10 s at 95°C, 30 s at 60°C, and 30 s at 72°C. A standard curve was plotted to calculate the efficiency of the real-time PCR primers. GAPDH was used as the housekeeping gene. mRNA expression was quantified by comparing CT methods (2 -ΔΔCT ), which was calculated using the normalization method. Amplified product specificity was analyzed using a melting curve. Table 1 Database and software information. Table 1 dummy alt text Database/Software Website/URL GeneCards https://www.genecards.org/ PubChem https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ STRING https://cn.string-db.org/ OMIM https://www.omim.org/ SuperPred https://prediction.charite.de/index.php DAVID https://davidbioinformatics.nih.gov/ SwissTargetPrediction http://swisstargetprediction.ch/ CTD https://ctdbase.org/ UniProt https://www.uniprot.org/ Venny 2.1.0 https://bioinfogp.cnb.csic.es/tools/venny/

Database and software information.

Western blot analysis was used to evaluate the expression levels of the Akt1 and p- Akt1 proteins. Primary myosatellite cells samples were lysed using protease inhibitor-containing radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) and centrifuged (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) for 15 min at 5000 rpm at 4°C, with subsequent collection of the supernatants. For western blot analyses, protein samples were separated using sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis on 10% acrylamide gels under denaturing conditions. The proteins were then transferred onto a 0.45 µm polyvinylidene fluoride membrane according to the manufacturer's instructions. After blocking the membrane with 5% (wt/vol) skim milk in Tris-buffered saline/Tween 20 for 1 h at 37°C, incubation was carried out overnight at 4°C with GAPDH (Proteintech, Wuhan, China), Akt1 (Cell Signaling Technology, Massachusetts, USA; ), and p-Akt1 (Cell Signaling Technology, Massachusetts, USA) antibodies. Subsequently, incubation with a peroxidase-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG antibody (Proteintech, Wuhan, China) was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Visualization was achieved using a chemiluminescence reagent (Pengguang Biotechnology Ltd., Chongqing, Hubei, China). Semi-quantitative protein expression analysis was conducted using Image J V1.8.0 software (National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, MD, USA) to analyze gray intensity.

The qPCR and Western blot results are presented as the mean ± standard error of mean (SEM). Statistical analysis and chart mapping were performed using the GraphPad software (GraphPad Prism 8.0, USA). Two-tailed Student's t-test was used to compare the two groups. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The GeneCards and OMIM databases yielded 8,687 and 187 MH-related targets, respectively. After deduplication, 8,706 MH-associated targets were retained. The Venny v.2.1.0 tool was used to identify the overlapping targets between UA and MH, presenting 92 shared targets ( Fig. 1 A). These intersecting targets suggest potential mechanisms, by which UA may act on MH. Fig. 1 Network pharmacology analysis. The 10 top BP, CC, and MF terms and 20 top KEGG pathways were visualized ( Fig. 2 A and B). GO enrichment analysis indicated that EGFR ( P = 2.8 × 10 -19 , Gene ratio = 0.174), insulin-like growth factor receptor ( P = 1.2 × 10 -18 , Gene ratio = 0.163), and ephrin receptor ( P = 2.5 × 10 -18 , Gene ratio = 0.163) signaling pathways in BP; receptor complex ( P = 6.4 × 10 -13 , Gene ratio = 0.163), cytosol ( P = 1.6 × 10 -8 , Gene ratio = 0.554), and nucleoplasm ( P = 2.1 × 10 -8 , Gene ratio = 0.457) in CC; and protein tyrosine kinase ( P = 3.8 × 10 -21 , Gene ratio = 0.196), transmembrane receptor protein tyrosine kinase ( P = 3.8 × 10 -21 , Gene ratio = 0.196), and glycosylphosphatidylinositol-linked ephrin receptor ( P = 1.2 × 10 -19 , Gene ratio = 0.185) activities in MF were significantly enriched. KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K)–Akt1 ( P = 1.1 × 10 -9 , Gene ratio = 0.22), FoxO1 ( P = 4.7 × 10 -9 , Gene ratio = 0.14), and mTORC1 ( P = 4.2 × 10 -3 , Gene ratio = 0.08) signaling pathways were significantly enriched. The PI3K–Akt1–mTORC1/FoxO1 cascade signaling network played a central regulatory role in the growth and development of skeletal muscles, and UA regulated the growth and development of skeletal muscles by affecting PI3K–Akt1–mTORC1/FoxO1 signaling. Molecular docking results showed that the binding pockets of UA and Akt1 were highly complementary (binding free energy, −7.7 kcal/mol; 96% homology to domestic chickens) ( Fig. 3 A). The Akt1 made nonbonded contacts with UA, forming π–π interactions with Tyr229 and hydrophobic interactions with hydrophobic amino acids such as Val164 and Met281 ( Fig. 3 B). Free energy decomposition analysis revealed that Val164 and Met281 contributed to more than 50% of the binding energy, further validating the reliability of the docking results ( Fig. 3 C). Fig. 3 Molecular docking studies reveal the binding of urolithin A (UA) to Akt1. (A) Homology modeling; (B) Interaction between UA and Akt1; (C) Free energy decomposition analysis between UA and Akt1. Fig 3 dummy alt text

The results showed that the root mean square deviation values of the null protein, ligand, and complex fluctuated between 0.1–0.8 nm throughout simulations and were finally stabilized at 0.6 nm, indicating their binding stability. To further assess the free energy changes of ligand–receptor binding, the MMGBSA method was used to calculate the binding free energies and predict the binding affinities of the protein–ligand complexes. sections.discussion:
In the broiler chicken industry, beta-adrenergic agonists such as ractopamine were once widely used to enhance meat production efficiency. However, drug residue issues triggered multiple food safety incidents ( Yin et al., 2023 ), prompting countries to explicitly ban the use of such drugs in animal husbandry ( Sakai et al., 2016 ; Chen et al., 2017 ). Against this backdrop, developing residue-free, highly compatible green growth promoters is an urgent requirement. UA, as the core end product of gut microbiota metabolism of pomegranate polyphenols, demonstrates significant potential to replace traditional β-adrenergic agonists in broiler health farming due to its natural non-toxicity, lack of bioaccumulation, and multi-target regulation of muscle homeostasis ( Zhang et al., 2023 ). We employ network pharmacology molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and primary muscle satellite cell functional assays to elucidate the molecular mechanism by which UA promotes broiler muscle development through interaction with the Akt1 signaling pathway.

Network pharmacology results reveal the multi-pharmacological potential of UA through 92 shared target points with MH. Among them, Akt1, TP53, and EGFR emerged as core hubs in the PPI network, reflecting their central roles in myogenesis. Akt1, a serine/threonine kinase, acts as a master regulator of muscle hypertrophy by acting downstream of insulin-like growth factor signaling to promote protein synthesis via mTORC1 ( Izumiya et al., 2008 ) and reduce protein degradation via FoxO1 ( Bodine et al., 2001 ). The high degree of centrality of TP53 suggests that UA may concurrently regulate apoptosis and cell cycle arrest, which are critical processes for balancing myoblast proliferation and differentiation ( Wan et al., 2020 ). EGFR, a tyrosine kinase receptor, further links UA to epidermal growth factor signaling, which is essential for the activation of satellite cells ( Liang et al., 2019 ). These multitarget effects align with the observed upregulation of myogenic regulatory factors (MyoD1, Myf5, and MRF4) ( Nalbandian et al., 2021 ) by UA treatment during both the proliferation and differentiation phases, emphasizing its dual role in enhancing myoblast recruitment and terminal differentiation.

KEGG enrichment analysis revealed significant enrichment in the PI3K-Akt, FoxO1, and mTORC1 signaling pathways. Furthermore, in vitro cellular experiments demonstrated that UA upregulates mRNA levels of Akt1, mTORC1 , and FoxO1 and protein levels of Akt1 and p-Akt1 during proliferation, suggesting a synergy between anabolic and catabolic drives ( Mullen et al., 2021 ; Jaiswal et al., 2022 ). However, during differentiation, UA suppressed mTORC1 while elevating FoxO1, which is a shift reflecting the transition from growth to stress adaptation ( Jaiswal et al., 2022 ). This biphasic regulation may reflect the ability of UA to finetune energy metabolism. Downregulation of mTORC1 during differentiation can prevent excessive protein synthesis and conserve resources for myofiber maturation ( Fortini et al., 2016 ). Upregulation of FoxO1 may enhance oxidative metabolism and autophagy, ensuring cellular quality control ( Cheng et al., 2009 ), a critical mechanism in fast-growing poultry breeds prone to metabolic stress. Molecular dynamic simulations confirmed the stability of this interaction. These residues lay within the kinase domain of Akt1, implying that UA stabilized its active conformation and subsequently enhanced its phosphorylation, a mechanism consistent with that of its promyogenic effects.

UA induced stage-specific metabolic reprogramming in myosatellite cells, orchestrating distinct regulatory effects on PDK4 and PFKFB3 for optimizing muscle development. During both proliferation and differentiation phases, UA significantly upregulated PDK4, a key inhibitor of pyruvate dehydrogenase redirecting glucose metabolism towards glycolytic flux and lactate production ( Luo et al., 2022 ). This adaptation probably fueled rapid biomass synthesis in proliferating myoblasts ( Wackerhage et al., 2022 ). Conversely, UA downregulated PFKFB3 specifically during the differentiation phase and inhibited glycolysis by limiting the synthesis of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate ( Zeng et al., 2022 ). The enhancement of PDK4-mediated pyruvate retention with the downregulation of PFKFB3 indicates that cells are in a metabolic reprogramming state ( Park et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2022 P; rimer et al., 2025 ). This metabolic regulation can maintain glycolysis-driven energy production during the proliferation phase to meet biosynthetic demands ( Wang et al., 2022 ), while shifting energy production toward fatty acid oxidation during the differentiation phase to support myofibrillar maturation ( You et al., 2023 ). Therefore, UA may counteract the metabolic rigidity observed in muscle hypoplasia by balancing glycolysis and oxidative metabolism pathways.

Breast muscle myopathies in broilers, often stemming from genetic, nutritional, or mitochondrial dysfunction, pose significant challenges to productivity and animal welfare ( Velleman, 2019 ). Our findings suggest that UA is a promising additive for mitigating breast muscle myopathy by leveraging its dual capacity to enhance myoblast proliferation (via Akt1/mTORC1 activation) and differentiation (via FoxO1 activation and metabolic reprogramming). The natural origin of UA aligns with the growing demand for antibiotic-free and sustainable feed additives ( Singh et al., 2022 ), offering a viable strategy for improving muscle yield in commercial broiler production and repairing of skeletal muscles in aging breeding stocks.
sections.conclusion: Our findings indicate that UA, a promising candidate, may mitigate skeletal muscle hypoplasia in broilers by activating the Akt1 pathway and stimulating muscle satellite cell proliferation and differentiation via the Akt1-mTORC1/FoxO1 axis, coupled with stage-specific metabolic regulation. As a natural and residue-free compound, UA represents a promising candidate for a sustainable strategy to improve muscle yield and health in commercial broiler production. However, the efficacy and application of this promising candidate necessitate further validation in animal models to confirm these in vitro observations and its practical utility under actual feeding conditions.
